metaTitle: Fence Construction in Ontario: A Guide
metaDescription: What to check before hiring a fence contractor in Ontario, including property line surveys, municipal height bylaws and material tradeoffs to weigh.
intro: Fencing disputes usually trace back to two things that get skipped at the start, an accurate property line and the local height bylaw. A contractor who confirms both before digging saves everyone a headache later, whether the job is a simple chain-link run or an ornamental aluminum fence along a front yard.
whatToLookFor: Willingness to work from a property survey rather than guessing the line
Familiarity with your municipality's fence height and setback bylaw
Experience with the specific material you want, wood, vinyl, chain-link or ornamental
Proper post depth and concrete footing for the local frost line
A plan for gate hardware and any slope or grade changes along the run
typicalCostNotes: Cost depends mainly on linear footage, material and how many gates or corners are involved, so a basic chain-link run typically costs less per foot than a tall wood privacy fence or ornamental aluminum. Difficult terrain, rock or tree roots along the line, and higher-end vinyl or cedar can push a quote well above a simple estimate, so ask for a per-foot breakdown before comparing bids.
questionsToAsk: Will you confirm the property line against my survey before setting posts?
Does this fence height and style comply with our municipal bylaw?
What is the post spacing and footing depth for this soil?
Who is responsible if we hit a neighbour's underground line during digging?
What happens if the ground has rock or roots along the fence line?
redFlags: No interest in seeing a survey or locating the actual property line
Dismisses the municipal height bylaw as unenforceable
Refuses to call Ontario One Call before digging post holes
